entry.title: madvise, Or Talking Back to the Kernel
entry.content:
In the OPT post I ended up at madvise() as the thing that already exists for "telling the kernel about the future", and I kept reading about it after, because it's kinda the only place in Linux where user space is officially allowed to have an opinion about its own pages. Everything else about virtual memory is the kernel deciding and you not knowing.

int madvise(void *addr, size_t length, int advice);

You give it a page-aligned range and a flag, and the kernel does something, or nothing, depends on the flag. That "or nothing" part is what makes it interesting to me.

hints that are actually hints

MADV_SEQUENTIAL and MADV_RANDOM describe how you're going to touch a file-backed mapping, so the kernel reads ahead more aggressively for sequential and basically turns readahead off for random. MADV_WILLNEED says I'll need this range soon, and for a file mapping the kernel starts reading it in asynchronously so the fault later is cheap (or doesn't happen). These are the polite ones, the kernel can ignore them and your program is still correct, just maybe slower.

MADV_HUGEPAGE is in the same family. If THP is set to madvise mode (common on servers), only ranges marked with this get huge pages, so it's an opt-in, and MADV_NOHUGEPAGE is the opt-out for the cases where huge pages hurt you, which happens more than people expect.

and one that is not a hint at all

MADV_DONTNEED sounds like the polite "I don't need this anymore, reclaim it if you want", but on private anonymous memory Linux throws the pages away right now, and the next access gets a fresh zero page.

size_t len = 64 << 20;
char *p = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
               MAP_PRIVATE | MAP_ANONYMOUS, -1, 0);
memset(p, 'a', len);

madvise(p, len, MADV_DONTNEED);
printf("%d\n", p[0]);   // 0, the 'a's are gone

So it's a free that keeps the mapping, which is actually useful (allocators use it exactly for this), but it's a command with a hint's name. POSIX has posix_madvise(POSIX_MADV_DONTNEED) which is supposed to be a real hint, and glibc on Linux just makes it a no-op, I'd guess because mapping it to the Linux one would silently destroy data in programs written for the POSIX meaning. lol.

MADV_FREE and the RSS confusion

MADV_FREE (4.5) is the lazier version. It tells the kernel these pages are garbage, but it doesn't drop them until there's memory pressure, and if you write to the page before that happens the kernel just cancels the free and keeps it. For an allocator this is nicer, because a lot of freed memory gets reused soon and with DONTNEED you'd pay a fault plus zeroing every time.

The problem is RSS doesn't go down. The pages are still counted against you until the kernel actually reclaims them, so tools and people looking at top think the program is leaking. Go switched its runtime to MADV_FREE and then switched back to MADV_DONTNEED by default a few versions later, mostly because of this, people saw memory "not being returned" and the monitoring and OOM decisions around containers believed RSS. I find that kinda funny, but I get it, if every dashboard shows the process growing nobody cares that the memory is technically free.

COLD and PAGEOUT

MADV_COLD and MADV_PAGEOUT came in 5.4 and these are closest to the OPT thing. COLD moves the pages to the inactive list so they're first in line for reclaim, while PAGEOUT reclaims them now, anon pages go to swap and clean file pages get dropped. Neither destroys data, the next access just faults it back in.

These came from Android, where the system knows an app went to the background long before the kernel's LRU figures it out. Which is the "the app knows more than the kernel" argument again, except the knowledge comes from the system watching the app, and the app itself doesn't say anything. And for that there's process_madvise() (5.10), which lets one process give advice about another process's memory through a pidfd. Only a few flags are allowed there (COLD, PAGEOUT, WILLNEED, COLLAPSE I think) and you need CAP_SYS_NICE plus ptrace-level access to the target, which makes sense, letting random processes push other people's memory to swap would be a fun attack.

This also kinda answers the trust question I had in the OPT post. Plain madvise only touches your own memory, so the worst a bad hint can do is hurt you, and the kernel doesn't need to trust you at all. The moment advice crosses a process boundary it needs permissions. I'm not sure that's a designed principle or it just happened that way, but it works.

the weird ones

Some flags aren't about caching at all and feel like they ended up in madvise because it was the syscall that takes a range. MADV_DONTFORK keeps a range out of the child after fork() (RDMA buffers need this), MADV_WIPEONFORK gives the child zeros instead of a copy, which is nice for RNG state or keys you don't want two processes to share by accident, and MADV_DONTDUMP keeps a range out of core dumps. MADV_MERGEABLE opts the range into KSM. MADV_POPULATE_READ / WRITE prefault the range so you don't take the faults later, which is basically MAP_POPULATE but for an existing mapping.

At this point it's less "advice" and more a drawer for per-range memory flags. I don't think that's bad, but the name stopped meaning much a while ago.

what I think about it

The thing I like is how small the leak in the abstraction is. The default is still the kernel deciding everything, and most programs never call madvise and that's fine. The programs that do call it are mostly allocators, runtimes, databases and Android, people who already know their memory better than the kernel and want a way to say so without taking over (which is what O_DIRECT and buffer pools do).

What's missing for me is anything with a notion of time, all of this is "now" or "soon" or "not anymore", nothing like "I'll need this in 10 seconds". Would the kernel even do anything useful with that? no idea, maybe not.

notes

  • addr has to be page-aligned, length gets rounded up to pages.
  • MADV_DONTNEED on shared or file-backed mappings doesn't zero anything, the next access just reads from the file/page cache again. The zeroing is the private anonymous case.
  • MADV_FREE only works on private anonymous memory.
  • MADV_COLLAPSE (6.1) synchronously collapses a range into huge pages instead of waiting for khugepaged.
  • MADV_REMOVE frees the backing store for shmem/tmpfs ranges, it punches a hole.
  • man 2 madvise is honestly pretty readable for once.

entry.title: Should malloc Know About Tiered Memory?
entry.content:
This started as a side thought in advanced systems class, we were talking about OS transparency in general and I kept coming back to malloc afterward, because it's the abstraction I use the most and never question, so this is me chewing on it more than a full argument.

malloc is blind

When you call malloc() you get a pointer, and the allocator has no idea if the physical page behind it is fast local DRAM or slower CXL-attached memory. glibc's allocator was built for a world where memory is mostly uniform, so it worries about arenas, chunks, brk vs mmap and lock contention, and leaves physical placement completely to the kernel. That was fine when the latency gap between memory was small, but machines now can have 2-3x differences between tiers, and from user space memory still looks flat.

the kernel fixes it later

The way tiered memory is handled today is the kernel treats slow memory like another NUMA node, watches which pages get accessed, and moves hot pages up to fast memory and cold ones down. It works, but it's always the same shape, allocate first, observe later, migrate if needed, so the system is always reacting.

And migration isn't free, you copy pages, update page tables, flush TLB entries, and if the kernel guesses wrong about what's hot you pay all that for nothing. I keep wondering how much of this goes away if the allocator just knew something before placing the memory.

the app already knows

void *hot_table = malloc(1 << 20);   // frequently accessed
void *log_buffer = malloc(1 << 20);  // rarely accessed
void *archive = malloc(100 << 20);   // mostly cold

Same call, same path as far as glibc is concerned, but these three are completely different in how hot they are. The application usually knows this already, and we throw that away and make the kernel figure it out again from access bits and sampling. Or even worse, trying to build AI models to handle this for us.

So one idea, not exotic at all, is to let the allocator take intent:

void *malloc_hot(size_t size);
void *malloc_cold(size_t size);

malloc_hot() could bind to the fast node using what already exists like mbind() and set_mempolicy(), and malloc_cold() goes straight to the slow tier, so instead of allocate, detect, migrate, you just place it right the first time and skip a lot of the copying.

is transparency still worth it here?

Virtual memory exists to hide where your bytes physically live, that's the whole point, but once the latency gap gets big enough placement starts mattering again whether we like it or not. You can keep it fully hidden and let the kernel grow more sampling and migration machinery, or leak a bit of the abstraction and let developers say hot or cold.

I don't know which is better tbh. Hints sound clean until people start labeling everything as hot because why not, and then what, the kernel ignores the hint? overrides it silently? Once you expose placement you also hand out responsibility for it, and I don't think most developers want that, even the ones who complain about performance.

Huge pages make it messier too. Inside one 2MB page only a small part might be hot, so moving the whole thing to fast memory wastes space, and the allocator doesn't even know how its allocations line up with huge page boundaries, the kernel can split or merge them later anyway. Page size, allocation and tier placement used to be separate concerns and they kinda aren't anymore.

I don't think transparency should go away, most programs don't care about this level of performance. But it doesn't have to be all or nothing, the default can stay hidden like today, and for the stuff that matters the allocator takes hints while the kernel keeps the right to override them when they're bad, or punish them!!!

entry.title: My monitor was dying
entry.content:
I got a new Dell monitor and a few days in I noticed a dim shadow in the top-left corner. It looked physical, like backlight bleed or panel uniformity issues, like I bought a defective unit.

blaming hardware first

When you see corner darkening you think hardware, so I wondered if I twisted the panel when mounting it, or if it was a bad cable or a backlight issue, and I ran the usual checks, but the built-in diagnostics were clean and different cables didn't help, and the shadow just sat there looking like it belonged to the panel.

the wayland test

I was about to start an RMA process when I thought I should at least try a different display stack. Logged into a Wayland session. Same laptop, same cable, same monitor.

Shadow gone.

So the monitor was fine. This had to be something in my X11 setup.

what changed

I tried to think about what was different, and I had updated ZWM (my window manager) a few days ago right around when this started, while everything else was the same, same picom config, same polybar, same everything. As a quick test, when I rolled back the ZWM changes the shadow disappeared, and when I restored them the shadow came back. So I broke something.

finding the actual cause

I started killing things to narrow it down, and disabling shadows in picom made the artifact go away, so it's definitely a shadow from some window. I re-enabled shadows and started killing windows one by one, and when I killed polybar the shadow disappeared instantly. So polybar was the source, but polybar was on my laptop screen and not on the external monitor, and I wasn't even looking at my laptop.

what I actually changed in ZWM

My WM update reimplemented the stacking order logic. The old code was a mess so I rewrote it to properly follow EWMH, which specifies that window types should stack in a particular order. _NET_WM_TYPE_DOCK windows (like polybar) are supposed to sit above most other windows.

Before my fix polybar wasn't stacked as high as the spec says it should be, and after my fix it was, and since picom draws shadows on windows, polybar's shadow was now rendering on top of other windows instead of under them. When Firefox or any bright window was near that corner of the screen, the shadow overlay looked exactly like panel dimming.

why the shadow crossed monitors

X11 treats the entire desktop as one big coordinate space where monitors are just rectangles positioned within it:

$ xrandr --listmonitors
Monitors: 2
 0: +*eDP 1920/302x1200/189+0+0  eDP
 1: +DisplayPort-0 2560/597x1440/336+1920+0  DisplayPort-0

My laptop screen is at x=0 and the external monitor starts at x=1920. Polybar sits at the top of the laptop screen and its shadow extends past its bounds, so if that extension reaches x=1920 it bleeds into the top-left corner of the external monitor. Shadows and blur effects don't know about monitor boundaries, they just work in global pixel coordinates, and that's where my "hardware defect" was.

fix

Added polybar to picom's shadow exclusion list. Shadow gone. Problem never came back.

takeaway

The monitor was fine the whole time and I almost returned working hardware because of a software shadow. Isolating layers is faster than spiraling through hardware returns, since the Wayland test took 30 seconds and told me everything I needed to know. I also learned that X11 multi-monitor is one big canvas and compositor effects don't stop at monitor boundaries unless you explicitly make them.

entry.title: Interrupts, Traps, and the Kernel Boundary
entry.content:
A syscall, a packet arriving on the NIC, and the timer firing all end the same way, the CPU stops running your code and starts running kernel code in ring 0. But they're not the same thing, and people use interrupt, trap, exception and fault almost interchangeably, which confused me for longer than I'd like to admit.

who caused it

The way I ended up sorting it is by asking who caused the switch.

If hardware caused it, it's an interrupt. The NIC got a packet, the disk finished a read, the timer says your time slice is up, and none of that has anything to do with the instruction you're running, you could be in the middle of a loop and it just happens to you, asynchronously.

If your own instruction caused it, it's synchronous, and that's the trap/exception family. Some of them you asked for, like a syscall or int3 from a debugger, and some you didn't, like a page fault, divide by zero, or an invalid opcode. Inside that family there's another split that actually matters, a fault can be fixed and the instruction retries (page fault loads the page, your load runs again and works), while an abort is unrecoverable and something is very wrong.

So interrupt is external and async, trap is internal and intentional, exception is internal and usually not intentional, and fault is the exception that gets retried. Different books will draw these lines a bit differently and I don't think it's worth fighting over.

where the CPU jumps

At boot the kernel fills the IDT, a table indexed by vector number, each entry holding a handler address and who's allowed to trigger it. When an interrupt or exception fires the CPU saves the instruction pointer, flags and stack, switches to ring 0 if needed, and jumps to the entry for that vector.

Syscalls on x86-64 are the exception to this btw. The old int 0x80 went through the IDT like any interrupt, but the syscall instruction skips it entirely and jumps to an address the kernel wrote into an MSR at boot, which is part of why it's faster.

top half, bottom half

Hardware interrupt handlers run with that interrupt line masked (or interrupts off entirely), so if they take long, other devices wait. Linux splits the work, the top half runs right away, does the minimum (grab the packet from the NIC, ack the device) and schedules the rest, and the bottom half (softirqs, tasklets, workqueues) does the actual work later with interrupts enabled. For networking the bottom half is where the packet goes up the whole stack, which is a lot of work to be doing "later".

what crossing costs

Every crossing means saving registers, switching to the kernel stack, and since Spectre also page table switches (KPTI) and other mitigations, which made syscalls noticeably more expensive overnight. A few hundred nanoseconds per syscall sounds like nothing until you do it hundreds of thousands of times a second. That's the reason io_uring batches I/O into shared rings, and why mmap is attractive, after the first fault there's no crossing at all. Most of the "fast I/O" ideas I've looked at are just different ways to cross this line less often.

notes

  • /proc/interrupts shows interrupt counts per CPU per device.
  • perf stat counts context switches, strace -c gives a quick syscall summary.
  • NMIs can't be masked, used for watchdogs and profiling.
  • The timer interrupt is what makes preemption possible, without it a busy loop would never give the CPU back.
  • Divide by zero becomes SIGFPE, which you can technically catch, but there's not much useful to do after.

entry.title: mmap: Mapping Files into Memory
entry.content:
mmap is one of those calls where the API is tiny and what happens behind it is most of the virtual memory system. You ask for a file (or just zeroed memory) to show up in your address space, you get a pointer back, and from then on you read and write the file like an array without any read() calls.

int fd = open("data.bin", O_RDONLY);
struct stat st;
fstat(fd, &st);

char *p = mmap(NULL, st.st_size, PROT_READ, MAP_PRIVATE, fd, 0);
// p[0..st.st_size-1] is the file now

nothing is loaded

The part that took me a bit to accept is that mmap doesn't read anything. The kernel just creates a VMA (a note saying "this range of addresses belongs to that file at that offset") and returns, so the actual loading happens later when you touch a page, it faults, the kernel pulls that page into the page cache, points your page table at it, and you continue like nothing happened. Second touch is a normal memory access, no kernel involved at all in it, and that's why it can be faster than read(), there's no copy into a user buffer and no syscall per access.

private vs shared

This is the flag that actually changes meaning. MAP_PRIVATE is copy-on-write, you read the file's pages but the first write gives you your own copy and the file never sees it. MAP_SHARED writes go into the page cache pages themselves, so other processes mapping the same file see them and they reach disk eventually, and "eventually" means whenever the kernel feels like it unless you call msync.

Add MAP_ANONYMOUS and there's no file at all, just zero pages. glibc malloc does this for big allocations (over 128KB by default), which is nice because munmap gives the memory straight back to the kernel, while memory from brk can only shrink from the top of the heap. Anonymous plus shared gives you memory that survives fork as shared between parent and child, and shm_open + mmap does the same for unrelated processes.

where it's good and where it hurts

It's good for reading big files with random access, and for read-only stuff many processes use, since they all map the same page cache pages, ten processes mapping a 1GB file don't cost 10GB. Shared libraries are loaded this way, and JITs use anonymous mappings with PROT_EXEC.

It hurts when you need control. The kernel decides when dirty pages hit disk, a page fault blocks your thread and you can't make it async, and if the file shrinks under you or the disk throws an I/O error you get SIGBUS instead of an error code, which is kinda horrible to handle. For databases all of this adds up, enough that most of them stopped using it. And for small files I don't think it's worth it, setting up the VMA and taking faults probably costs more than one read(), though I never measured it.

Appending to a file is also awkward, the mapping has a fixed size so you ftruncate to grow the file and remap, and at that point write() is just simpler.

notes

  • MAP_POPULATE prefaults everything at map time, so mmap gets slow but later accesses don't fault.
  • MAP_FIXED puts the mapping at your exact address and silently replaces whatever was there. MAP_FIXED_NOREPLACE is the safer one.
  • PROT_NONE pages are good as guard pages, mprotect changes protection later.
  • MAP_HUGETLB for huge pages, less TLB pressure.
  • madvise() tells the kernel how you'll access the range (MADV_SEQUENTIAL, MADV_RANDOM, MADV_WILLNEED).
  • Exiting without munmap is fine, the kernel cleans up. Long-running stuff should unmap tho, or VMAs pile up.

entry.title: Multi-Monitor Support in a Tiling WM
entry.content:
I figured I should write down how multi-monitor actually works in ZWM.

The core idea is that each monitor is independent, so it has its own desktops, its own focused window, and its own layout state, and when you switch desktops you switch on that monitor only, and when you tile windows you tile within that monitor's usable area.

the data model

Monitors are a linked list, and each monitor holds an array of desktops, a pointer to the currently focused desktop, physical dimensions from RandR, padding for bars, and some identity info:

struct monitor_t {
    desktop_t         **desktops;   // array of desktops
    desktop_t          *desk;       // currently focused desktop
    monitor_t          *next;       // next monitor in list
    rectangle_t         rectangle;  // physical dimensions
    padding_t           padding;    // strut padding (for bars)
    xcb_randr_output_t  randr_id;
    uint32_t            id;
    bool                is_focused;
    bool                is_primary;
    // ...
};

Three global pointers track state:

monitor_t *head_monitor = NULL;  // start of linked list
monitor_t *curr_monitor = NULL;  // currently active monitor
monitor_t *prim_monitor = NULL;  // primary monitor (usually where bar lives)

Most operations use curr_monitor. When you spawn a window, it goes to curr_monitor->desk, and when you switch desktops, you're switching curr_monitor->desktops[n].

detecting monitors at startup

At startup, ZWM checks what's available:

  1. RandR if present (preferred)
  2. Xinerama if RandR isn't there
  3. Fallback to the whole screen as one monitor
query_xr = xcb_get_extension_data(wm->connection, &xcb_randr_id);
query_x  = xcb_get_extension_data(wm->connection, &xcb_xinerama_id);

if (query_xr->present) {
    using_xrandr = true;
    randr_base = query_xr->first_event;
    xcb_randr_select_input(wm->connection, wm->root_window,
                           XCB_RANDR_NOTIFY_MASK_SCREEN_CHANGE);
}

If RandR is present, I also subscribe to screen change events, which is how hotplug works later. For RandR, the setup iterates outputs, skips disconnected ones, and creates a monitor_t for each connected output with a valid CRTC, where each monitor gets its rectangle from the CRTC geometry.

desktops per monitor

Each monitor gets its own set of desktops:

curr->n_of_desktops = conf.virtual_desktops;
curr->desktops = malloc(sizeof(desktop_t *) * curr->n_of_desktops);

for (int j = 0; j < curr->n_of_desktops; j++) {
    desktop_t *d = init_desktop();
    d->id = (uint16_t)j;
    d->is_focused = (j == 0);
    curr->desktops[j] = d;
}
curr->desk = curr->desktops[0];

So if you have 2 monitors and 5 desktops configured, you actually have 10 desktops total, 5 on each monitor. Desktop 1 on monitor 1 is completely independent from desktop 1 on monitor 2.

Desktop switching only affects the current monitor:

for (int i = 0; i < curr_monitor->n_of_desktops; ++i) {
    curr_monitor->desktops[i]->is_focused = (curr_monitor->desktops[i]->id == id);
    if (curr_monitor->desktops[i]->id == id) {
        curr_monitor->desk = curr_monitor->desktops[i];
    }
}

which monitor is current

This is pointer-driven, meaning the monitor under the mouse pointer is the current one. When a new window appears, I check where the pointer is and update curr_monitor:

if (multi_monitors) {
    monitor_t *mm = get_focused_monitor();
    if (mm && mm != curr_monitor) {
        curr_monitor = mm;
    }
}

get_focused_monitor() queries pointer position and finds which monitor rectangle contains it. Same thing happens on enter notify and motion notify events: when the pointer crosses into a different monitor, curr_monitor updates.

geometry and layout

Each monitor has a usable area which is the physical rectangle minus strut padding (for bars like polybar):

int32_t x = m->rectangle.x + m->padding.left;
int32_t y = m->rectangle.y + m->padding.top;
int32_t w = (int32_t)m->rectangle.width - m->padding.left - m->padding.right;
int32_t h = (int32_t)m->rectangle.height - m->padding.top - m->padding.bottom;

Layouts compute within this usable area, and gaps and borders are subtracted:

rectangle_t usable = get_usable_area(m);
r->x = usable.x + conf.window_gap;
r->y = usable.y + conf.window_gap;
r->width  = usable.width  - 2 * conf.window_gap - 2 * conf.border_width;
r->height = usable.height - 2 * conf.window_gap - 2 * conf.border_width;

Fullscreen is also monitor-aware, so a fullscreen window fills its monitor rather than the whole X11 screen:

monitor_t *m = get_monitor_by_window(win);
rectangle_t r = m ? m->rectangle : curr_monitor->rectangle;
resize_window(win, r.width, r.height);
move_window(win, r.x, r.y);

cycling monitors

Keyboard shortcut to move focus between monitors:

if (m && m != curr) {
    move_mouse_to_monitor(m);
}

I warp the pointer to the target monitor, and the enter/motion handlers then update curr_monitor. I don't directly assign curr_monitor here because I want the pointer position to stay in sync with which monitor is active.

hotplug

RandR sends XCB_RANDR_SCREEN_CHANGE_NOTIFY when monitors connect or disconnect:

if (using_xrandr &&
    event_type == randr_base + XCB_RANDR_SCREEN_CHANGE_NOTIFY) {
    handle_monitor_changes();
    return 0;
}

handle_monitor_changes() detects three cases, a new monitor connected which means creating a monitor node, initializing desktops, and adding it to the linked list, a monitor geometry changed which just updates the rectangle, and a monitor disconnected, which is the tricky one.

When a monitor disconnects, its windows need to go somewhere, so I merge them into another monitor:

for (int i = 0; i < om->n_of_desktops; i++) {
    desktop_t *od = om->desktops[i];
    desktop_t *nd = nm->desktops[i];
    // traverse old desktop tree
    // for each window: unlink from old, transfer to new
    // rearrange target tree
}

Windows from desktop 1 of the old monitor go to desktop 1 of the remaining monitor, and then I destroy the old monitor node.

notes

  • RandR is the modern way, Xinerama is legacy but still needed for some setups
  • The coordinate space is global: monitor at x=0 is leftmost, next monitor starts at x=1920 (or whatever)
  • Strut padding comes from EWMH, bars like polybar set _NET_WM_STRUT_PARTIAL and the WM respects it
  • Primary monitor is queried from RandR, and if not set, I default to head of the list

entry.title: EWMH and ICCCM: What a WM Actually Needs to Implement
entry.content:
EWMH and ICCCM are the two specs that define how window managers and clients talk to each other through properties on windows, atoms, and message formats. Without them every app would need to know specifically how to talk to your particular WM, and with them apps can just assume standard behavior. Every WM implements some subset of these, and here's what actually matters.

ICCCM: the old one

ICCCM is the Inter-Client Communication Conventions Manual from 1988 and it covers the basics, so WM_NAME holds the window title, WM_CLASS holds the instance name and class name that you match windows to rules with, WM_HINTS carries the input focus model and icon and initial state, WM_NORMAL_HINTS carries size hints like min/max size and aspect ratio and resize increments, WM_PROTOCOLS lists which protocols the client supports such as WM_DELETE_WINDOW, and WM_STATE is the current state (normal, iconic, withdrawn).

Of those the ones that actually matter for a basic WM are a smaller set. WM_DELETE_WINDOW is the one where, if the client lists it in WM_PROTOCOLS, you send a ClientMessage instead of killing the window so the app can save unsaved work before it closes. WM_TAKE_FOCUS is for apps that handle focus themselves, where you send a ClientMessage when you want to focus the window and the app focuses its own input field. WM_NORMAL_HINTS is size hints again, and some apps set a minimum size or a fixed aspect ratio, so a tiling WM can mostly ignore this but floating windows should respect it. WM_STATE is something you're supposed to set on managed windows because some apps check it, with NormalState for visible, IconicState for minimized, and WithdrawnState for not managed. WM_CLASS is critical for window rules since the class name tells you what app this is, which is what you use to auto-float dialogs or send certain apps to specific desktops.

ICCCM is showing its age tho, it doesn't know about multiple desktops, fullscreen, maximized state, struts (docking bars), or window types, and that's what EWMH adds.

EWMH: the modern one

EWMH is the Extended Window Manager Hints and it's what most modern apps and WMs actually use.

root window properties

These go on the root window and describe the overall WM and desktop state. _NET_SUPPORTED is the list of EWMH atoms you support, which apps check to know what features work. _NET_CLIENT_LIST is all managed windows and _NET_CLIENT_LIST_STACKING is the same thing in stacking order from bottom to top, and pagers and taskbars use both. _NET_CURRENT_DESKTOP is which desktop is active, _NET_NUMBER_OF_DESKTOPS is how many exist, and _NET_DESKTOP_NAMES is their names. _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW is the currently focused window. _NET_SUPPORTING_WM_CHECK points to a child window with _NET_WM_NAME set to the WM name, and apps use it to detect whether a compliant WM is running at all.

client window properties

Apps set these on their own windows. _NET_WM_NAME is the UTF-8 window title and you should prefer it over WM_NAME. _NET_WM_WINDOW_TYPE says what kind of window it is, with _NET_WM_WINDOW_TYPE_NORMAL for a regular app window, _DOCK for panels and bars like polybar, _DIALOG for dialogs, _SPLASH for splash screens, _UTILITY for toolbars and palettes, and _NOTIFICATION for notification popups. This is how you know to auto-float dialogs or keep docks above other windows, and getting it right makes a huge difference in how the WM feels.

_NET_WM_STATE is the set of current state flags, so _NET_WM_STATE_FULLSCREEN for fullscreen, _MAXIMIZED_HORZ and _MAXIMIZED_VERT for maximized, _HIDDEN for minimized, _ABOVE and _BELOW for always on top or bottom, and _DEMANDS_ATTENTION for the urgency hint. _NET_WM_DESKTOP is which desktop the window belongs to, where 0xFFFFFFFF means sticky and visible on all of them. _NET_WM_STRUT_PARTIAL is reserved screen space that docks set to tell the WM not to tile windows in their area. _NET_WM_PID is the process ID, which is useful when you want to know which process owns a window.

client messages

Apps send these to the WM to request things and the WM decides whether to honor them. _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW requests focus for a window and pagers use it. _NET_CLOSE_WINDOW requests a close and taskbars use it. _NET_WM_STATE requests a state change like toggling fullscreen, and the message carries the action (add, remove, toggle) plus which state atoms. _NET_CURRENT_DESKTOP requests a desktop switch and _NET_WM_DESKTOP requests moving a window to a different desktop.

what I actually implemented

For a tiling WM the spec is big but you don't need all of it. The parts that have to be there are _NET_SUPPORTED to advertise what you support, _NET_SUPPORTING_WM_CHECK to prove you're EWMH compliant, _NET_CLIENT_LIST because pagers need it, _NET_CURRENT_DESKTOP and _NET_NUMBER_OF_DESKTOPS for desktop switching, _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW for focus tracking, _NET_WM_STATE handling and especially fullscreen, _NET_WM_WINDOW_TYPE to identify docks and dialogs and splashes, _NET_WM_STRUT_PARTIAL to respect space reserved by bars, and WM_DELETE_WINDOW to close windows properly.

The nice-to-haves are _NET_WM_NAME for UTF-8 titles, _NET_CLIENT_LIST_STACKING for stacking-aware pagers, _NET_DESKTOP_NAMES for named workspaces, and _NET_WM_DESKTOP for moving windows between desktops. The things you can skip in a tiling WM are _NET_WM_STATE_MAXIMIZED_* since tiling windows are already maximized in a sense, and _NET_WM_MOVERESIZE for interactive resize and move, which isn't really relevant when everything tiles.

handling state changes

When an app sends a _NET_WM_STATE client message, data.l[0] is the action (0 remove, 1 add, 2 toggle), data.l[1] is the first state atom, and data.l[2] is an optional second state atom. So a fullscreen toggle comes out roughly like this:

if (action == _NET_WM_STATE_TOGGLE) {
    if (is_fullscreen(win)) {
        unfullscreen(win);
    } else {
        fullscreen(win);
    }
}

You also need to update the property on the window afterwards so other apps like pagers and taskbars can see the current state.

the annoying parts

Order matters, because some apps expect you to set properties in a specific order during the initial manage, and Java is notorious for this. UTF-8 is another one, since _NET_WM_NAME is UTF-8 but WM_NAME might be latin1 or something else entirely, so you have to handle both. Struts are per-monitor and _NET_WM_STRUT_PARTIAL has 12 values covering left, right, top, bottom, and a start and end for each, so a bar on the left side of monitor 2 has a specific left strut with start_y and end_y bounding its position. Desktop indices trip people up too, because apps expect 0-indexed desktops where _NET_CURRENT_DESKTOP = 0 is the first one, and some early EWMH implementations got this wrong.

notes

  • ICCCM: https://tronche.com/gui/x/icccm/
  • EWMH: https://specifications.freedesktop.org/wm-spec/latest/
  • xcb_ewmh.h provides helpers for getting/setting these properties
  • If something isn't working, check what you advertise in _NET_SUPPORTED, apps check this
  • Run xprop on windows to see what properties they set, useful for debugging

entry.title: How a Window Manager Talks to X11
entry.content:
When I started writing ZWM I didn't understand how a window manager intercepts window creation, because applications create windows by talking to the X server directly so how does the WM get in the middle? turns out the WM is just another X client, but it asks the server to redirect certain events to it instead of handling them normally.

everything is events

X11 is event-driven, so when something happens like a key press or a window being created or resized the server generates an event, and clients tell the server which events they want to receive by setting event masks on windows.

In XCB, event masks are just bit flags you OR together:

#define S_NOTIFY    (XCB_EVENT_MASK_SUBSTRUCTURE_NOTIFY)
#define S_REDIRECT  (XCB_EVENT_MASK_SUBSTRUCTURE_REDIRECT)
#define SUBSTRUCTURE (S_NOTIFY | S_REDIRECT)

#define PROPERTY_CHANGE (XCB_EVENT_MASK_PROPERTY_CHANGE)
#define FOCUS_CHANGE    (XCB_EVENT_MASK_FOCUS_CHANGE)
#define ENTER_WINDOW    (XCB_EVENT_MASK_ENTER_WINDOW)
#define LEAVE_WINDOW    (XCB_EVENT_MASK_LEAVE_WINDOW)
#define BUTTON_PRESS    (XCB_EVENT_MASK_BUTTON_PRESS)

You combine whatever you need for a specific window.

the root window

There's one special window called the root window that covers the entire screen, and all other windows are children of it.

The root window is how the WM gets control, because by setting certain masks on it the WM intercepts events that would normally be handled by the server. In ZWM I define what the root window listens for:

#define ROOT_EVENT_MASK \
    (SUBSTRUCTURE | BUTTON_PRESS | FOCUS_CHANGE | ENTER_WINDOW)

SUBSTRUCTURE is the key part. That's SubstructureNotify | SubstructureRedirect.

SubstructureRedirectMask

When you set XCB_EVENT_MASK_SUBSTRUCTURE_REDIRECT on the root window, you're telling the X server not to automatically handle requests that affect the root window's children, and to send them to you instead.

What gets redirected:

  • XCB_MAP_REQUEST, client wants to show a window
  • XCB_CONFIGURE_REQUEST, client wants to move or resize
  • XCB_CIRCULATE_REQUEST, client wants to change stacking order

Without this mask, when an app wants to map a window the server just shows it wherever the app asked, but with the mask you get a MapRequest event and decide what to do, which is how tiling WMs work, where the app says "make me 800x600" and the WM intercepts it, ignores the size, and tiles it wherever it should go.

only one WM

Only one client can hold SubstructureRedirectMask on root at a time, so if another client already has it you get BadAccess, which is how you detect if another WM is already running.

what clients listen for

Client windows need different masks than root. In ZWM:

#define CLIENT_EVENT_MASK \
    (PROPERTY_CHANGE | FOCUS_CHANGE | ENTER_WINDOW | LEAVE_WINDOW)
  • PROPERTY_CHANGE, know when window title or state changes
  • FOCUS_CHANGE, track focus in and out
  • ENTER_WINDOW and LEAVE_WINDOW, for focus-follows-mouse

the event loop

XCB uses xcb_wait_for_event() which blocks until there's an event, and my event loop in ZWM looks like this:

static void
event_loop(wm_t *w)
{
    xcb_event_t *event;
    while (!should_shutdown && (event = xcb_wait_for_event(w->connection))) {
        if (event->response_type == 0) {
            _FREE_(event);
            continue;
        }
        if (handle_event(event) != 0) {
            uint8_t type = event->response_type & ~0x80;
            char   *es   = xcb_event_to_string(type);
            _LOG_(ERROR, "error processing event: %s ", es);
        }
        _FREE_(event);
    }
}

The & ~0x80 strips the "sent by SendEvent" flag. You dispatch on the event type.

dispatching events

I use a table-driven approach where each event type maps to a handler function:

static const event_handler_entry_t _handlers_[] = {
    // map request - window wants to be displayed
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_MAP_REQUEST, handle_map_request),
    // unmap notify - window was hidden
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_UNMAP_NOTIFY, handle_unmap_notify),
    // destroy notify - window was killed
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_DESTROY_NOTIFY, handle_destroy_notify),
    // client message - EWMH requests from other apps
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_CLIENT_MESSAGE, handle_client_message),
    // configure request - client wants to resize/move
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_CONFIGURE_REQUEST, handle_configure_request),
    // enter notify - cursor entered window
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_ENTER_NOTIFY, handle_enter_notify),
    // button press - mouse button clicked
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_BUTTON_PRESS, handle_button_press_event),
    // key press - keyboard input
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_KEY_PRESS, handle_key_press),
    // property notify - window property changed
    DEFINE_MAPPING(XCB_PROPERTY_NOTIFY, handle_property_notify),
};

Then dispatch is just a loop through the table:

size_t n = sizeof(_handlers_) / sizeof(_handlers_[0]);
for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    if (_handlers_[i].type == event_type) {
        return _handlers_[i].handle(event);
    }
}

the important events

MapRequest is a window wanting to appear, so you decide if you manage it, where it goes, and what size it gets.

ConfigureRequest is a client wanting to move or resize, and for a tiling WM you mostly ignore the requested geometry, but for floating windows you might honor it.

ClientMessage is the EWMH protocol, where other apps send these to request things like:

  • _NET_WM_STATE, toggle fullscreen, above, below
  • _NET_ACTIVE_WINDOW, bring window to front
  • _NET_CLOSE_WINDOW, close a window from a pager
  • _NET_CURRENT_DESKTOP, switch desktop

PropertyNotify is a window title changing, WM hints updating, and so on.

EnterNotify is the cursor entering a window, used for focus-follows-mouse.

reparenting vs non-reparenting

When a WM "manages" a window there are two approaches. Reparenting WMs create a frame window for each client, and the client window becomes a child of the frame:

Before managing:
  root -> client

After managing (reparenting):
  root -> frame -> client

The frame is where decorations go, so the title bar, borders, and close button, and when you move the frame the client moves with it. i3 does this, drawing frames around windows and using them for the colored borders and title bars. Non-reparenting WMs leave the client as a direct child of root:

After managing (non-reparenting):
  root -> client

There's no frame, so if you want borders you manipulate the client window's X11 border directly with xcb_configure_window and XCB_CONFIG_WINDOW_BORDER_WIDTH. dwm does this and ZWM does too. The tradeoff is that reparenting gives you more flexibility for decorations but adds complexity, since you have to handle ReparentNotify events, manage the frame lifecycle, and deal with apps that don't like being reparented, while non-reparenting is simpler but you're limited to what X11 window borders can do, which is basically solid color rectangles.

Some apps behave differently under reparenting WMs. Java apps are the worst, they historically had issues with reparenting and they still do, and they expect things to work a certain way in a certain order. Chrome and Electron apps sometimes need hints. Most modern apps handle it fine though.

what I learned

The WM isn't special at all, it's just a client that grabbed redirect on root first. The X server doesn't even know what a "window manager" is, it just follows the rules about who gets which events.

notes

  • XCB is lower level than Xlib. No magic, you manage memory yourself.
  • ICCCM and EWMH define conventions. Not enforced, just expected.
  • xcb_wait_for_event() blocks. For non-blocking, use xcb_poll_for_event().
  • Event response type 0 means error, not a real event.
